why: Once the object leaves the moving bus it keeps the bus's horizontal velocity, and gravity acts on it vertically downwards. It therefore carries a constant horizontal velocity and a uniformly accelerated vertical motion at the same time, and those two independent motions combine into a parabolic path. That is exactly the definition of projectile motion. It is not uniform circular motion, because nothing supplies a centripetal force towards a fixed centre and the object never turns through a circle. It is not rectilinear motion, and equally not motion in one dimension \(-\) those two options describe the same straight-line situation in different words, and both fail for the same reason: the object moves horizontally and vertically at once, so its displacement needs two coordinates and its path is curved, not straight.

In uniform circular motion the particle covers equal arc lengths in equal times, so the MAGNITUDE of its velocity never changes \(-\) that magnitude is the speed, and it is the one quantity in the list that stays constant. Every other listed quantity is a vector whose direction changes continuously as the particle goes round. The velocity is always tangential, so although its magnitude is fixed its direction turns through \(360^\circ\) each revolution, and a vector of changing direction is not constant. The acceleration is centripetal, of fixed magnitude \(\dfrac{v^{2}}{r}\) but always directed towards the centre, so its direction turns too. The displacement measured from any fixed point changes from instant to instant, and over one full revolution it even returns to zero. So only the speed qualifies.

A conical pendulum is a bob on a string that sweeps out a cone, with the string making a constant angle \(\theta\) with the vertical. The bob therefore stays at a fixed depth below the support and traces a HORIZONTAL circle of radius \(r = l\sin\theta\). The two forces on it are the string tension \(T\) and its weight \(mg\); the vertical components balance, \(T\cos\theta = mg\), while the unbalanced horizontal component \(T\sin\theta\) supplies exactly the centripetal force needed to keep it turning. Since that resultant has no tangential component, the speed cannot change, so the motion is uniform motion in a horizontal circle. It is not motion in a vertical circle, because the bob never rises or falls once the cone is established, and the two rectilinear options are wrong outright \(-\) the path is a closed circle, not a straight line.

Read the question carefully: it asks which statement is NOT correct, so the answer is the single false one. For uniform acceleration, \(v = u + at\) is a first-degree equation in \(t\), so a graph of \(v\) against \(t\) is a straight line. The claim that the velocity-time graph is nonlinear therefore contradicts this and is the false statement. Checking the other three confirms they are all true and so cannot be the answer: the velocity-time graph being linear is the same fact just stated correctly; acceleration is the slope of that graph, since \(a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\), and for uniform acceleration that slope is constant, which is precisely why the line is straight; and the area under a velocity-time graph is \(\int v\,dt\), which is the displacement.

The velocity of A relative to B is what an observer riding on B measures for A. Working in a common frame, that is A's velocity minus B's velocity, \(\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B\), which is the correct choice. The subtraction is the whole point: if A and B move identically then \(\vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B = 0\), correctly saying B sees A at rest. The sum \(\vec{v}_A + \vec{v}_B\) fails that test immediately, giving \(2\vec{v}_A\) instead of zero, and it is not even the right idea \(-\) it would describe a closing rate for oppositely directed motion, not a relative velocity. The expression \(\vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_C + \vec{v}_B\) drags in the irrelevant third particle C and, worse, ADDS B's velocity rather than subtracting it. The remaining expression \(\vec{v}_C - \vec{v}_A\) is the velocity of C relative to A, a different pair of particles in the reverse order.
